title: The Boy Who Buried His Fear
summary: Whenever Rafe is afraid, he locks the fear in a chest and buries it in the garden, so he never has to feel it. But fears buried in the dark do not die — they grow, fed by never being faced, until the garden is full of monsters, and Rafe must learn that the only way past a fear is through it.

chapters.title: The Chest in the Garden
chapters.body:
Rafe was ten, and he hated being afraid, and he had found what seemed like the perfect way never to feel it.

He had been given, by a strange traveling tinker, a small iron chest with a heavy lock — and the tinker had told him it was no ordinary chest. "This one holds feelings," the tinker had said. "Whatever feeling troubles you, you can put it in here, and lock it away, and you won't feel it anymore. Out of sight, out of heart." And then the tinker had added, as tinkers in these stories always do, a warning that Rafe did not heed: "But mind — some feelings ought to be felt, not locked away. Especially fear. A fear you never feel is a fear you never face. And a fear never faced does not simply vanish, boy. It waits. And it grows."

Rafe barely listened, because he had just been handed a way to never feel afraid again, and that was all he wanted. Rafe was an anxious boy, and fear troubled him often — fear of the dark, fear of failing, fear of the big dog on the lane, fear of a hundred things large and small. And now he had a chest that could take those fears away.

So the next time Rafe felt afraid — it was a fear of a coming test at school — he took the iron chest, and he put the fear inside it, and he locked it. And at once the fear was gone. He couldn't feel it anymore. He walked into his test the next day with no fear at all, because the fear was locked in the chest. And then, because it seemed wrong to leave a chest full of fear sitting in his room, he took it out into the garden and buried it, deep in the earth, so the locked-away fear was out of sight entirely.

It worked so well that Rafe did it again. And again. Every time a fear troubled him, he put it in the iron chest — which always seemed to be back in his room when he needed it, empty and waiting, however many times he'd buried it — locked it, and buried it in the garden. Fear of the dark: into the chest, into the ground. Fear of the big dog: buried. Fear of disappointing his father: buried. One by one, Rafe took every fear he felt and locked it away and buried it in the dark earth of the garden, and walked through his life feeling, at last, no fear at all.

He thought he had solved the oldest problem there is. He felt brave — not because he had faced anything, but because he had buried everything that frightened him. And his garden filled, season by season, with buried chests full of locked-away fears, sleeping in the dark under the soil.

He did not think about what the tinker had said. He did not think about what happens to fears that are buried instead of faced. He did not notice, at first, that the ground of his garden had begun, in places, to stir.

chapters.title: What Grew in the Dark
chapters.body:
It began with sounds in the garden at night.

Faint, at first — a scratching, a rustling, a low sound like something breathing under the soil. Rafe told himself it was animals. But the sounds grew, night by night, and then the ground itself began to change. The earth over the buried chests bulged and cracked. Strange dark shapes began to push up out of the soil — not plants, but something else, something wrong, growing from the buried chests like terrible flowers. And Rafe realized, with a cold dread, what was happening. The tinker had warned him. A fear buried in the dark does not die. It grows.

Every fear Rafe had locked away and buried — instead of vanishing — had been sitting in the dark earth, unfaced, unfelt, and in that darkness it had grown. Fed by never being confronted, watered by avoidance, each buried fear had swollen and twisted and taken root, and now they were pushing up out of the garden as monsters — dark, half-formed, terrible things, each one grown from a fear Rafe had refused to feel. The small fear of the dark he'd buried years ago had become a great shapeless shadow-thing that loomed at the garden's edge. The fear of the big dog had become a snarling beast far larger and more frightening than any real dog. The fear of disappointing his father had grown into a towering figure of disapproval and shame. Every fear he'd buried had grown, in the dark, into something far worse than the fear had been when he first felt it.

And here was the terrible thing Rafe understood, watching his garden fill with the monstrous grown-up shapes of his own buried fears: they were so much bigger now. When he'd first felt each fear, it had been small — a manageable, ordinary fear, the kind everyone feels and faces and gets past. The fear of the test had been just a flutter of nerves. The fear of the dog had been just a child's unease. If he had simply felt those fears, and faced them, they would have passed, the way fears do when you face them — shrinking, once looked at, to their true small size. But he hadn't faced them. He'd buried them, unfaced, and in the dark of never-being-looked-at, they'd grown monstrous, swollen far beyond their real size, into things far more frightening than the fears themselves had ever been.

Rafe ran to find the old tinker, and by some luck found him still passing through, and begged him to explain how to get rid of the monsters in his garden.

"You can't get rid of them the way you made them," the tinker said gravely. "You buried your fears to avoid feeling them, and that's exactly what grew them. You can't un-bury a fear by burying it deeper, or by running from these monsters — running is just more avoidance, and avoidance is what feeds them. There's only one way to make a buried fear shrink back down to its true size, boy, and it's the very thing you've spent all these years avoiding." The tinker looked at him steadily. "You have to dig them up. And face them. Feel each fear you buried — really feel it, look right at it — because a fear only grows in the dark of being unfaced. The moment you face it, look straight at it, and feel it all the way through, it stops growing. And then it shrinks. A faced fear always shrinks to its true size, which is almost always far smaller than the monster it became in the dark. But you have to dig them up and face them. Every one. There's no other way."

And Rafe looked at his garden full of towering monsters — years of buried, grown fears — and understood that to save himself, he would have to do the single thing he'd built his whole life around avoiding: he would have to feel his fears.

chapters.title: The Only Way Through
chapters.body:
Rafe took a shovel out into his monster-filled garden, and he began, with his heart pounding, to dig up his fears and face them.

He went to the smallest monster first — the shadow-thing grown from his old fear of the dark. He was terrified to approach it; every instinct screamed at him to run, to bury it deeper, to avoid it as he always had. But he made himself walk up to it, and dig up the chest it had grown from, and open the lock, and — this was the hard part, the part he'd avoided his whole life — feel the fear inside. He let himself feel his fear of the dark, fully, looking straight at it instead of locking it away. And the moment he did — the moment he faced the fear and felt it all the way through instead of burying it — the towering shadow-monster shuddered, and stopped growing, and began to shrink. Smaller and smaller it drew, as Rafe faced it, until it was just what it had always truly been underneath: a small, ordinary, manageable fear of the dark, the kind every child feels, no monster at all. And once it was small again, and faced, it simply... faded, and was gone. Not buried. Not avoided. Faced, felt, and released.

Rafe understood, then, the whole truth of it. The burying had never made his fears go away. It had only made them grow, in the dark, unfaced, into monsters far worse than they truly were. And the only way to actually be free of a fear was the exact opposite of what he'd been doing: not to bury it, but to dig it up; not to avoid feeling it, but to feel it fully; not to lock it away in the dark, but to bring it into the light and look straight at it. Because a fear faced shrinks to its true size, and a fear felt all the way through loses its power, and a fear brought into the light cannot grow the way it does in the dark. The only way past a fear, it turned out, was through it.

So Rafe faced them all. One by one, he dug up every buried chest, and opened every lock, and felt every fear he had spent his life avoiding. It was the hardest thing he had ever done, and the most frightening — he had to feel, all at once, years of accumulated fears he'd never let himself feel. He faced the monster grown from his fear of the dog, and felt the fear, and watched it shrink to its true small size and fade. He faced the towering figure grown from his fear of disappointing his father, and felt that fear fully — and it too, once faced, shrank down to something small and manageable and human, and lost its terrible power. Every fear he'd buried, he dug up and faced and felt, and every one, once faced, shrank and faded, because that is what fears do when you finally stop avoiding them and look them in the eye.

By the time he was done, the garden was clear. Every monster was gone — not buried deeper, but truly gone, dissolved by being faced. And Rafe stood in his emptied garden, exhausted and shaken and, for the first time in his life, genuinely brave. Not the false bravery of having buried everything frightening — the real bravery of having faced it. He had felt all his fears, all the way through, and survived, and come out the other side, and there was nothing left buried in the dark to grow into monsters. He was free — not because he'd avoided his fears, but because he'd finally faced them.

Rafe gave the iron chest back to the tinker, who took it with a knowing nod. "You won't be needing it anymore," the tinker said. "You've learned the thing it can't teach — the thing it can only teach by going wrong. A feeling locked away isn't gone; it just grows in the dark. And a fear, most of all, has to be felt to be freed. Bury it, and it becomes a monster. Face it, and it shrinks to nothing. There's no way around a fear, boy. There never was. The only way is through."

And Rafe grew up brave — truly brave, in the only way anyone ever is. Not fearless; he still felt fear, often, as everyone does. But he never buried a fear again. When fear came, he faced it — looked straight at it, felt it all the way through, let it shrink to its true size and pass. And because he faced his fears instead of burying them, they never grew into monsters, and never ruled him, and never filled his life with towering dark shapes grown from everything he'd refused to feel. He had learned the thing that the anxious and the avoidant never learn, and that the brave discover: that a fear faced is a fear that shrinks, and a fear felt is a fear set free, and that the only way past the things that frighten us — the only way that has ever worked, or ever will — is straight through the middle of them, with open eyes, feeling every step.
